overview:
For more than a thousand years, the eastern half of the Roman world went on functioning after the western half had broken apart. Its capital was Constantinople, refounded by Constantine I on the Bosporus in 330, and its people never stopped calling themselves Romans — Rhomaioi — and their state Romanía. The label "Byzantine" is a retrospective invention of early modern western scholars, taken from Byzantion, the old Greek town on the site; some historians now avoid it as misleading. Even the starting date is a matter of convention rather than evidence. The division of the empire between the sons of Theodosius I in 395 is one common marker, but others begin with Constantine around 330, and still others push the real break to the seventh century, when the empire lost Syria, Egypt and North Africa and became a smaller, Greek-speaking, thoroughly Christian state. There is no consensus, and the disagreement is partly about what one thinks the empire essentially was.

The arc that follows is one of repeated near-collapse and repeated recovery. Justinian I (527–565) reconquered Italy, North Africa and part of Spain, codified Roman law in the Corpus Iuris Civilis, and rebuilt Hagia Sophia — then saw plague and exhausting war with Persia drain the gains. In the 630s and after, Arab armies took the empire's richest provinces and twice besieged the capital; the century that follows is thinly documented, and the administrative and military system that emerges from it looks markedly different from what went in. The eighth and ninth centuries were consumed by the iconoclast controversy over religious images, and by missionary expansion that carried Orthodox Christianity and a Slavic literary language into the Balkans and, eventually, the Rus'. Under the Macedonian emperors the empire expanded again and its art, scholarship and diplomacy reached a height that impressed visitors from Baghdad to the Latin west. Defeat by the Seljuk Turks at Manzikert in 1071 opened Anatolia to permanent settlement by outsiders; the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204 and shattered imperial authority into competing successor states.

The restored empire after 1261 was a regional power living among stronger neighbours — Venice and Genoa controlled its trade, Serbs and Bulgarians its Balkan hinterland, and the rising Ottoman state absorbed what remained of Anatolia. Its last century was spent seeking western military help at the price of church union, which its own clergy and populace largely rejected. On 29 May 1453 Mehmed II's army took Constantinople; the last emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting. Throughout, the empire had sat at the hinge of the medieval world, trading and fighting with Persians, Arabs, Turks, Bulgars, Rus', Normans and Italians, and passing on Roman law, Greek learning and a model of Christian monarchy in every direction.
significance: Byzantium is the reason the classical world did not simply stop. Its scribes copied the Greek texts — Plato, Aristotle, Euclid, the historians — that later reached Renaissance Italy, often carried by refugees from the fifteenth-century collapse; its jurists preserved Roman law in the form that would underlie most European legal systems; its missionaries gave the Slavic world an alphabet, a liturgy and a church that still shapes Russia, Ukraine, Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania and Greece. For centuries it also acted as the eastern Mediterranean's shock absorber, its walls and diplomacy shaping how far Arab and later Turkish power expanded and when. And its end was itself a beginning: the Ottoman Empire took Constantinople as its capital and much of Byzantine administrative and architectural practice with it, while Moscow's later claim to be a "third Rome" shows how long the imperial idea outlived the state.
coverage: Written from general reference works (Wikipedia, Britannica), the Met's Byzantine art timeline, and Fordham's collection of translated Byzantine sources; this dataset attaches no events at all to the story, so nothing here can be shown on the map. The surviving record is itself uneven: the seventh and eighth centuries are poorly documented, provincial archaeology in Anatolia is barely tapped, the iconoclast emperors survive mainly through the writings of their victorious opponents, and figures like Justinian reach us through Procopius, who wrote both official praise and a venomous secret attack on the same reign.
